messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

On the night of a routine hazmat drill in 1976, Michael—an 72‑year‑old African American veteran of the U.S. Coast Guard—found himself in the middle of a sudden toxic spill. Thick, bitter smoke erupted from a containment tank in the ship’s galley, the acrid scent flooding the air before the emergency alarm blared. He saw his fellow crew members stumble, a white cloud of chemical vapor curling around them, and heard the frantic shouts of the command center as the ship’s captain shouted “Evacuate!” The scene was so vivid that, years later, Michael could still see a photograph of the gas plume in his mind, every detail as sharp as if he were looking at a picture on a wall. After the incident, Michael’s first realization was that he could not cope with even a slight disturbance. The belief that he had lost his capacity to handle the world’s stressors became a core negative appraisal. This sense of helplessness fed into a constant perception of threat. At home, the quiet of the night felt like a looming danger, as if something was waiting in the dark. Even the most ordinary silence—his wife’s soft breathing, the refrigerator hum—sent his heart racing, and he felt compelled to be on guard inside his own house. The fear that the world was unsafe, especially when it seemed to be silent, amplified his sense of threat beyond the initial event. In the months that followed, the memories of the chemical spill resurfaced with alarming regularity. Each flash of the gas cloud on the mental screen triggered a wave of threat. The memory replayed like a film, frame by frame: the scream of the captain, the taste of ozone, the wet footprints in the galley. The vividness of these images made Michael feel as though the danger were present again, and the threat he sensed intensified. When a familiar scent of bleach drifted from a nearby window, the film would cut to that scene, and he would feel his chest tighten, sweat breaking out across his brow. The overwhelming nature of these memories was also the source of Michael’s deeper negative appraisals. Whenever he tried to recall the event, the flood of emotion was so intense that he would have to stop mid‑thought. The sense of being unable to handle even the slightest upset was reinforced by each failed attempt to remember. This cycle of over‑overwhelmed recall solidified his belief that he was low in coping ability and that he could never manage such distress again. Because the threat lingered in Michael’s mind, it continually drew him back to those memories. The mere sensation of danger—whether triggered by a sudden silence or a distant alarm—would bring his mind to the hazmat drill. The recurring threat served as a cue, pulling him into the filmic replay of the event. The more often the threat surfaced, the more often the memory flooded back, reinforcing each other in a tightening spiral. Over time, Michael began to avoid any setting that might bring the chemical scent or even the quiet of the night; he would keep the lights on, carry a whistle, and stand by the front door at night. The ongoing sense of threat kept the negative appraisals alive as well. Each moment he felt unsafe, the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could not cope was reinforced. Michael began to avoid thinking about the incident altogether, convinced that if he could not endure the thought, it would only worsen his sense of threat. He would shift conversations away from any hint of danger, telling his wife that nothing “could be worse.” The avoidance extended to his retirement routine: he refused to join the local harbor patrol group, fearing a sudden chemical spill, and even declined to visit his niece’s home, where she kept her house quiet to maintain a calm environment. Now, after years of living under that constant, unseen threat, Michael has finally decided to seek help. The weight of isolation at home, the inability to enjoy quiet moments with his wife, and the physical exhaustion from always being on guard have taken a toll. He fears that without intervention he will continue to miss out on simple pleasures and that his sense of safety will never be restored. He hopes to find a way to let the memories fade from the film reel, to ease the physical reactivity he experiences at the slightest reminder, and ultimately to feel safe again, both in his own home and in the world outside it.
